Government & extension nutrition sites

Your tax dollars paid for these. No ads, no sponsors, no “sponsored post” — just recipes and guidance that someone with a nutrition degree reviewed. Blurb note: two lines each — what it is, why you’d flip to it tonight.

The picks

MyPlate Kitchen — USDA

A big, free, ad-free database of tested healthy recipes with built-in nutrition facts, many on a budget and SNAP-friendly. Tonight use: filter by ingredient or cost, get a recipe that already knows its nutrition numbers — no reverse-engineering needed.

SNAP-Ed Connection recipe search — USDA

The recipe index behind SNAP nutrition education: cheap, standard-ingredient, family-scale recipes with cost and prep filters. Tonight use: the narrow search (main ingredient + budget + minutes) is one of the fastest “I’m shopping right now” tools on this list.

Nutrition.gov cooking & meal planning

A hub page from the USDA portal that rounds up the government’s cooking and planning resources in one clean list. Tonight use: when you want the reference page rather than one recipe — it links healthy-cooking guides, food safety, and budget tips.

Food Hero recipes — Oregon State Extension

University extension recipe site with tested low-cost recipes, family-tested and sorted by ingredient, time, and cost. Tonight use: the extension-test-recipe standard shows here: forgiving proportions, real pantry ingredients, no hard-to-find anything.

Spend Smart. Eat Smart. — Iowa State Extension

Low-cost recipes with per-serving cost estimates, plus honest “is this actually cheaper” notes from extension educators. Tonight use: the per-serving cost line next to each recipe makes sideways-between-similar-dinner decisions easy.

DASH Eating Plan — NHLBI

The NIH’s heart-healthy DASH plan: sample menus, weekly planner goals, and heart-friendly recipe ideas — evidence-based, not fad. Tonight use: when someone in the house is watching blood pressure or sodium, these are the dinners a cardiologist actually describes.
